authors: Agatha Kratz, Max J. Zenglein, Andreas Mischer, Gregor Sebastian, Armand Meyer (Rhodium Group and MERICS)
title: Chinese Investment Rebounds Despite Growing Frictions: Chinese FDI in Europe: 2024 Update
method: descriptive deal-level tracking of Chinese M&A and greenfield FDI in the EU and UK (Rhodium China Cross Border Monitor), combined with Commission screening statistics and a hand-collected list of publicly disclosed screening cases (section 3)
outcomes: Chinese FDI volumes and composition; share of screening notifications involving Chinese investors; outcomes of disclosed screening cases
headline: The share of EU-screened transactions involving Chinese investors rose to 6% in 2023 (from 5.4% in 2022) even as Chinese M&A fell; the authors count 9 publicly disclosed screening cases involving Chinese firms in 2024 (12 in 2023, 16 in 2022), with blocks or forced divestments in semiconductors, batteries and gas turbines.
summary_plain: Chinese takeovers of European companies have shrunk to a fraction of their 2016 peak, while new Chinese-built factories (mostly for electric cars and batteries) are growing. More of the deals that governments review now involve Chinese buyers, and several sensitive deals were blocked or unwound in 2024.
quality: Descriptive monitoring; screening is one of several drivers (capital controls, geopolitics) and no attempt is made to isolate its effect; case list admittedly partial because most reviews are confidential.
interested_party: Rhodium Group is a commercial research consultancy; MERICS is an independent think tank (foundation-funded)

title: Europe's door to Chinese tech investment is still ajar
venue: Centre for European Reform, CER Insight (4 March 2026)
method: structured qualitative assessment with case evidence (blocked or unwound Chinese semiconductor acquisitions 2021-2025) and descriptive FDI data (Rhodium/MERICS, AidData)
outcomes: blocking of Chinese acquisitions in sensitive tech; shift from M&A to greenfield; geographic shift towards member states with looser screening
headline: Since the 2019 framework, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK have blocked or unwound Chinese acquisitions of sensitive semiconductor assets, but Chinese FDI has shifted to greenfield projects in permissive member states - Hungary took 44% of Europe-bound Chinese investment in 2023 and 33% in 2024 - which the M&A-focused screening framework barely covers.
summary_plain: CER finds that European governments have largely stopped Chinese takeovers of sensitive tech firms, but the screening system, which was optional and uneven from 2020, does little about Chinese companies building their own factories, which now go mainly to countries with weaker screening such as Hungary.
quality: Policy analysis with case evidence and descriptive data; no causal identification; attributes the geographic shift partly to looser screening without testing it.

authors: Samuele Greco, Chiara Pollio, Lauretta Rubini, Alessandra Vecchi
title: Screening degli IDE europei e investimenti green cinesi in UE
method: legal analysis of Regulation 2019/452 and its roll-out plus descriptive trend analysis of Chinese green-sector FDI in Europe 2019-2024
outcomes: Chinese green-sector FDI trends before and after the screening framework
headline: The paper documents trend shifts in Chinese green-sector FDI into Europe between 2019 and 2024 alongside the roll-out of the EU screening framework (no effect size reported in the abstract).
summary_plain: An Italian study that describes how the EU's investment-screening rules were rolled out and how Chinese investment in green technologies in Europe changed from 2019 to 2024.
quality: Descriptive only, in Italian; only the abstract was available (no full text in repository); no causal design.

searched: Round 3 think tank sweep: 2 WebSearches (Bruegel, CEPS, CER, Transparency International on AMLR/AMLA, beneficial ownership access, single rulebook implementation evidence). Found only law-firm/vendor notes and a TI EU legal explainer (Feb 2026, no data). AMLR applies only from July 2027, so no ex-post think tank assessment exists yet.

authors: Arcep (Autorité de régulation des communications électroniques, des postes et de la distribution de la presse)
title: Bilan du cadre de régulation symétrique des réseaux en fibre optique (FttH) - évaluation notifiée à la Commission européenne en application de l'article 61(5) du CECE
venue: Arcep evaluation (notified 10 February 2026; final version April 2026), with European Commission opinion
method: national regulator's ex-post evaluation required by EECC Art. 61(5) of symmetric access obligations: descriptive statistics on FttH coverage, take-up and investment, plus public consultation of stakeholders
outcomes: FttH coverage, share of fixed accesses on fibre, investment, competition
headline: At 30 June 2025, 41.6 million of 44.9 million premises (93%) were connectable to fibre, up from 15% in 2015; fibre rose from 5% to 75% of fixed accesses 2015-2025 and cumulative public and private investment is estimated at close to EUR 50 billion; the Commission raised no objections.
summary_plain: France's telecoms regulator reviewed the rules that oblige fibre network builders to share their networks with rivals, a review the EU Code requires. It found that these rules, together with public subsidies, helped bring fibre to 93% of homes and businesses, and stakeholders largely agreed they should be kept.
quality: Self-evaluation by the regulator of its own framework (predates the EECC, in place since 2009; review mandated by EECC Art. 61(5)); descriptive, no counterfactual; the Commission and stakeholders endorsed it.

authors: BEREC (Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications)
title: BEREC Report on Switching and Termination of contracts (BoR (26) 76)
method: questionnaire of 30 national regulators on national implementation of EECC Art. 105-107 (switching, number porting, contract termination), descriptive cross-country comparison
outcomes: switching and porting procedures, commitment periods, automatic contract renewal, device locking, complaints
headline: BEREC finds the EECC switching framework implemented efficiently but with remaining disincentives: 24 NRAs report automatic prolongation of fixed-term contracts, 10 report that locked handsets are still sold, and 18 member states port mobile numbers within one working day.
summary_plain: European telecoms regulators surveyed how the EU Code's rules on changing provider and ending contracts work in each country. The rules are largely in place, but problems remain, such as contracts that renew automatically, locked phones and providers trying to keep customers during the switch.
quality: Descriptive regulator survey; no outcome measurement of switching rates and no counterfactual; BEREC explicitly does not give an opinion on the results.

authors: Dutch Authority for the Financial Markets (AFM) and De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB)
title: Digital dependence of the financial sector
venue: AFM and DNB joint report (20 October 2025)
method: supervisory assessment based on interviews with banks, insurers, payment providers, asset managers and ICT vendors, plus desk analysis
outcomes: concentration on non-EU ICT providers; unintended effects of DORA on ICT supplier market; adequacy of DORA oversight
headline: Interviewed institutions report that smaller ICT suppliers are withdrawing from the financial sector because they cannot or will not comply with DORA and that DORA encourages using fewer providers, raising concentration; the supervisors judge DORA's critical-provider oversight insufficient for geopolitical risks while noting it prompted firms to demand uptime guarantees, exit options and audit rights.
summary_plain: The Dutch financial supervisors found that banks and insurers rely heavily on a few US cloud companies. Firms told them that the new EU resilience rules have pushed some small IT suppliers out of the sector and led firms to use fewer suppliers, which could make the concentration problem worse.
quality: Qualitative, interview-based (number of interviews not stated); early evidence less than a year after DORA applied; supervisors are DORA competent authorities.

searched: Round 3 think tank sweep: 2 WebSearches (cep, Tax Foundation, CASE, ifo, ZEW on ViDA; early national e-invoicing mandates in Belgium/Poland enabled by ViDA). Only vendor and consultancy timelines found; no ex-post assessment. Main ViDA obligations apply from 2027-2030.

Round 3: 2 WebSearches (.eu registrations, abuse, Brexit revocation, eligibility of EU citizens abroad, any study/evaluation 2023-2025). Only industry news and law-firm notes on the existing 2022 Commission report; no think tank or academic ex-post study of Regulation 2019/517.

authors: WODC (Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek- en Datacentrum, Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security); external research team (Rotterdam) not named in summary
title: Evaluation of Implementation Act on the Regulation on Terrorist Content Online - Final report (English summary)
method: statutory ex-post evaluation: document review, 28 semi-structured interviews, workshops, case studies of Germany, Ireland and Sweden, plus removal-order statistics
outcomes: removal orders issued and complied with; over-removal; administrative burden; governance; effect on terrorist content online
headline: About 330 removal orders were issued by the Dutch authority (ATKM) in 2024-2025, almost all complied with within the one-hour deadline (around 20% of all EU removal orders), with no fines, appeals or exposure decisions; but about three-quarters of flagged content falls outside scope and no effect on overall terrorist content can be shown.
summary_plain: A Dutch government-commissioned evaluation found that when the Dutch authority orders a platform to remove terrorist content, it is almost always taken down within an hour and there is no sign of lawful content being removed by mistake. But it cannot show that the law has reduced terrorist content online overall, partly because there was no baseline and content moves to closed channels.
period_geography: Sept 2023 - June 2026; Netherlands (with comparisons to DE, IE, SE)
quality: Mixed-methods implementation evaluation; no baseline or counterfactual for impact; only the English summary was read.
interested_party: Commissioned by the ministry responsible for the implementing act

title: Terrorist Content Online Regulation Transparency Report 2025 (Article 8 transparency report and Article 21(1) monitoring report)
venue: An Garda Síochána report (year under review 2025, as of March 2026)
method: statutory statistical transparency report of the Irish competent authority
outcomes: removal orders issued, scrutinised and implemented
headline: Ireland's competent authority issued one removal order in 2025, and the content was taken down; no removal orders were scrutinised under Article 4.
summary_plain: Ireland hosts the EU headquarters of many big platforms, yet its police issued only one order under the EU terrorist-content law in 2025, which was obeyed.
quality: Bare counts only; shows very low use of removal orders by the authority in the main hosting jurisdiction.

title: Hungary's Online Political Advertising Market in Transition: Monitoring Before and After the TTPA's Entry into Force
venue: Liberties monitoring brief, Phase I (3 November 2025)
method: monitoring study of Meta and Google ad libraries and media reports in Hungary around the TTPA's application date (10 October 2025), drawing on Political Capital analyses
outcomes: undeclared or mislabelled political ads after platform bans; ad-library transparency
headline: After Google and Meta stopped political ads ahead of the TTPA, Fidesz-linked ads kept running under non-political labels, and Google retroactively reclassified 60-70% of the past year's ads by major Hungarian parties into non-political categories, reducing transparency.
summary_plain: A civil liberties NGO tracked online political ads in Hungary as the new EU rules started. Political ads did not disappear when Google and Meta 'banned' them; they were relabelled or went undeclared, and the platforms' public ad archives became less useful for watchdogs.
quality: Case-based monitoring of one country; relies partly on third-party analyses and media; measures platform responses to the TTPA rather than the regulation's own rules.
interested_party: Campaigning civil liberties NGO that argued against the platform bans

title: To Ban or not to Ban? Online Political Advertisements in the Hungarian Election (TTPA monitoring brief, Phase III)
method: monitoring of Meta, Google/YouTube and TikTok ad repositories and accounts in the run-up to Hungary's April 2026 parliamentary election
outcomes: circumvention of platform political-ad bans; platform enforcement
headline: The pro-government group NEM launched 183 political ads on Meta after the ban (at least EUR 200k); Meta classified 84% as political, but not immediately, and Google's repository listed no breaches, making monitoring impossible.
summary_plain: In Hungary's 2026 election, political ads still ran on Facebook after Meta's ban, using tricks such as not labelling them, proxy pages and small influencers. Liberties says the EU rules will only work if platforms enforce their bans and the EU builds its planned public ad database.
quality: Single-country monitoring; only the landing-page summary was read (Phase III PDF link not found); access limits on Google and TikTok data.

authors: Political Capital Policy Research and Consulting Institute
title: A tiltás ellenére 14 fideszes jelölt sikeresen futtatott Facebook-hirdetéseket januárban (Despite the ban, 14 Fidesz candidates successfully ran Facebook ads in January)
method: analysis of Meta Ad Library data for all 106 Fidesz constituency candidates, 1-25 January 2026
outcomes: political ads run despite Meta's post-TTPA ban; share caught by Meta
headline: 14 of 106 Fidesz constituency candidates ran 181 ads on Facebook in January 2026; Meta classified only 19 as political and stopped them, while 162 passed its filters.
summary_plain: A Hungarian think tank checked Facebook's ad archive and found that ruling-party election candidates ran over 160 political ads in a single month despite Meta's ban on political ads, introduced in response to the EU's new rules.
quality: Simple count from ad-library data for one party and one month; tests platform enforcement after the TTPA rather than TTPA compliance itself; read in Hungarian, also reported by Lakmusz.

title: Trade Secrets as a Resource for Value Creation. A study investigating the impact of the EU directive (2016/943) on companies' value creation
venue: Master's thesis, Chalmers University of Technology (Department of Technology Management and Economics)
method: qualitative study: semi-structured interviews with companies, lawyers and professors plus before/after comparison of trade-secret court cases in Denmark, Sweden, Ireland and the UK
outcomes: firms' trade secret management; court case characteristics before and after transposition
headline: Interviewees and the case comparison suggest the Directive improved companies' trade-secret management and their ability to create value from trade secrets, though whether it increased use of trade secrets is unclear (no quantified effect).
summary_plain: A Swedish master's thesis interviewed companies and lawyers and compared court cases before and after the EU trade secrets law. It concludes that companies now manage their confidential know-how better, but the evidence is limited.
period_geography: c.2014-2020; DK, SE, IE, UK (interviews EU-wide)
quality: Student thesis; small qualitative sample, few quantitative elements; weak evidence; included only because no other new study was found.
